result.summary: Pindar praises Argos, its heroes and its women, then celebrates Theaios of Argos for his many athletic victories. He links the family's gift for athletics to the Dioskouroi and tells how Kastor was killed by Idas, and how Polydeukes shared his immortality with his brother.

scenes.title: Editor's note
scenes.summary: The editor notes that the ode is wrongly called Nemean and commemorates a victory at the Hekatombaia in Argos.

scenes.title: Glories of Argos
scenes.summary: Pindar praises Argos for its heroes, its gods and its beautiful women.

scenes.title: Victories of Theaios
scenes.summary: Pindar lists Theaios' wins at the Argive games, the great festivals and neighbouring cities, and prays to Zeus for him.

scenes.title: The Twin Gods
scenes.summary: The athletic gift of the family is tied to the visit of Kastor and Polydeukes. The twins live alternately in heaven and beneath the earth.

scenes.title: Death of Kastor
scenes.summary: Idas kills Kastor over oxen, and Lynkeus spots the twins. Polydeukes kills Lynkeus, and Zeus destroys Idas with a thunderbolt.
scenes.stakes: Kastor's life is lost and Polydeukes is in mortal danger from the sons of Aphareus.

scenes.title: Polydeukes' Choice
scenes.summary: Polydeukes begs to die with his brother, and Zeus offers him a choice. He shares his life with Kastor, and Zeus revives Kastor.
scenes.stakes: Polydeukes must choose between full immortality and sharing his brother's fate.

alias_notes.explanation: Son of Kronos, a patronymic title for Zeus.
Polydeukes is called Tyndareus' son though Zeus is his true father.
Apollo is named by his mother.

notable_quotes.reason: A short, memorable statement of divine reliability.
Polydeukes' lament on how rare faithful companions are.

analysis.text: The ode links athletic excellence to heroic ancestry, so Theaios' wins are part of Argos' long tradition of glory.
The Dioskouroi myth presents brotherly loyalty as worth more than immortality, a model of friendship in hardship.

legacy.text: Kastor and Polydeukes (Castor and Pollux) became the twin stars of Gemini, and the shared-immortality tale was widely retold in later antiquity.

fun_facts.text: Pindar gives a different version of Kastor's death than the Cypria epic, in which Kastor was killed in the oxen quarrel with Idas and Lynkeus.

language_notes.text: "Sing Graces!" is an address to the Graces (goddesses of charm and favour), asking that they be sung; the clause is compressed and its syntax awkward.
Hypermnestra alone of the fifty daughters of Danaos spared her husband Lynkeus on the wedding night, disobeying her father's order to kill him.
The prophet is Amphiaraos, son of Oikleus; Zeus's thunderbolt opened the earth and swallowed him and his chariot during the war against Thebes.
"Grey-eyed goddess" is Athena's regular epithet, though this translation uses it without naming her. She made Diomedes immortal, according to tradition.
Zeus fathered Herakles on Alkmene and Perseus on Danaë, both Argive women; this is his "testimony" to their beauty.
Zeus took Amphitryon's likeness to visit Alkmene, who then bore Herakles; Amphitryon had meanwhile defeated the Teleboai, a raiding people.
"Distaste of men" means that people tire of long praise or grow resentful, so the poet must stop.
The bronze shield was the prize at the Argive games, the Heraia, held in honour of Hera; hence the sacrifice of oxen to her.
Pytho is Delphi; Isthmos and Nemea are the other great festival sites. Together with Olympia these formed the four major Greek games.
"Gave work for the Muses' plough" means he supplied poets with victories to celebrate in song.
The ordinance of Herakles is the Olympic games, held at Pisa, traditionally founded by Herakles.
The Athenian prize was olive oil in decorated baked-clay jars (Panathenaic amphorae); Theaios also won such a prize at Argos.
Proitos was a legendary king of Argos, so "city of Proitos" means Argos.
The sentence is elliptical: the cities listed are the places which also gave bronze prizes, and the Lykaion games were Arcadian.
"Mete out" means to apportion or distribute; the twins allot good fortune in contests.
Kastor was mortal and died in a fight; Polydeukes, son of Zeus, shared his immortality with him, so they alternate between heaven and underground.
"Wroth" means angry; "smite" means strike. Both are archaic. "Him" refers to Kastor.
"Leto's son" is Apollo, though here the text's Polydeukes is in view as the chaser; the translator's note marks the identification as debated.
"Drave" is an archaic past tense of "drive"; "give back" means retreat.
"Kronion" means son of Kronos, a title for Zeus.
Zeus is Polydeukes' true father; Kastor's father was the mortal Tyndareus, husband of Leda, so Kastor is mortal.
"Art so hot" means so zealous or passionate in your brother's cause.
"Unsealed the eye" means Zeus opened Kastor's eyes, restoring him to life and speech.

context_notes.text: The Hekatombaia was an Argive festival of Hera, named for the hundred oxen sacrificed; it included athletic games.
Argos was Hera's chief cult centre, and Danaos was its legendary king, whose fifty daughters are the Danaids.
Hebe, goddess of youth, married Herakles after his deification; her mother is Hera, goddess of marriage.
Theaios' mother's family was linked to the Tyndaridai, the sons of Tyndareus, namely Kastor and Polydeukes, and to the Graces.
Pamphaes was an ancestor of Theaios' family who, in tradition, hosted the Twin Gods, explaining the family's athletic talent.
Therapnai was a place near Sparta where the twins were worshipped and thought to be buried.
Taÿgetos is the mountain range overlooking Sparta; Lynkeus was famed for sight so sharp he could see through objects.
The thunderbolt is Zeus's characteristic weapon.
Athene is goddess of wisdom and war; Ares is the god of war. Olympus is the home of the gods.

literary_notes.text: The sentence strings together "many" Argive glories in a catalogue, building a sense of abundance.
Calling Amphiaraos "the storm-cloud of war" pictures him as a looming, threatening force in battle.
"King of the immortals" names Zeus by his rank, stressing the honour that Amphitryon's house received.
Victories become a plough that the Muses work, picturing poetry as farming sustained by athletic success.
Pindar speaks as if he were a kinsman, showing the poet's pride and personal tie to the victor's city.
This brief statement stands out after long sentences, giving a moral statement that gods keep faith with their descendants.
The poet draws a general moral from the brothers' fate: contending with the stronger brings ruin.
Polydeukes' grief is voiced as a general truth about friendless men, deepening his plea.
Two lots are balanced: deathless Olympus alone versus shared life and death beneath the earth and in heaven, highlighting brotherly loyalty.
"Of the brazen mail" is a fixed descriptive phrase marking Kastor as a warrior as he revives.
